chunks: And from him (Al-Shaykh) from Ibn Isa from Al-Qasim Al-Sayqal who said:

Umm Ali sent a letter to him asking about uncovering the head in the presence of the servant. She said to him, 'Your Shias have differed with me regarding this; some of them said there is no harm, and some of them said it is not permissible.' So he (peace be upon him) wrote back: 'You asked about uncovering the head in the presence of the servant; do not uncover your head in his presence, for that is disliked (makruh).'

key_terms.أُمُّ عَلِيٍّ: Umm Ali (a specific female figure, often identified as the mother of Imam al-Hasan or a distinct companion)
key_terms.بَيْنَ يَدَيِ الْخَادِمِ: In the presence of the servant
key_terms.مَكْرُوهٌ: Disliked (a category of legal ruling in Shia fiqh, between permissible and forbidden)

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling on a woman uncovering her head in front of a male servant?
ai.summary: This correspondence from Umm Ali highlights the practical application of *adab* (etiquette) within the domestic sphere, reflecting the scholarly nuance between permissibility and preferred decorum in early Shia jurisprudence. The Imam’s ruling of *makruh* (disliked) rather than *haram* (forbidden) underscores a flexible approach to social modesty, distinguishing between strict legal obligation and spiritual refinement. This incident is often cited to demonstrate the Imam’s role in guiding the community on subtle social norms beyond the core pillars of faith.
